hints: Look at A1 and A2 first. One is an aldehyde with a $\text{CHO}$ group and one is a ketone. Which classic test gives a silver mirror or brick red precipitate only with aldehydes?
Remember that the same A pair could also be distinguished the opposite way. Which test gives a yellow precipitate only with a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group?
Compare B1 and B2. Both are ketones, but only one contains a $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ group. Which reagent tests specifically for that group?
For B, think about what colour or precipitate you see when that methyl carbonyl test is positive.
Compare C1, a ketone, with C2, an ester. Which reagent gives a coloured precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone but not with an ester?
Recall the typical colour of the precipitate formed with that carbonyl reagent.
Compare D1, a tertiary alcohol with no $\text{C=C}$, with D2, an unsaturated alcohol. Which orange aqueous reagent tests for a $\text{C=C}$ bond?
Think about what happens to the colour of that orange reagent when it adds across a $\text{C=C}$ bond and which compound, D1 or D2, will cause it.
walkthrough:
Sort out the A pair, aldehyde versus ketone**
Look closely. A1 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, propanal, an aldehyde. A2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, propanone, a ketone. Aldehydes are easily oxidised, ketones are not. So Tollens reagent gives a silver mirror only with A1, Fehling's gives a brick red precipitate only with A1, acidified dichromate goes orange to green only with A1. Alternatively you can use the iodoform test the other way round, A2 contains $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ so gives yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$, A1 does not.

Sort out the B pair, methyl ketone versus non methyl ketone**
B1 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, pentan-2-one, it has $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$. B2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, pentan-3-one, it does not. Only the methyl ketone gives the triiodomethane reaction. Warm with alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ and B1 gives a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$, B2 stays colourless.

Sort out the C pair, ketone versus ester**
C1 is hexan-3-one, a ketone with $\text{C=O}$. C2 is propyl propanoate, an ester, no aldehyde or ketone carbonyl reactivity in this test. 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, 2,4-DNPH, gives a red, orange or yellow precipitate with aldehydes and ketones only. So C1 gives the coloured precipitate, C2 gives no precipitate.

Sort out the D pair, saturated alcohol versus unsaturated alcohol**
D1 is 1-methylcyclobutan-1-ol, a tertiary alcohol with no $\text{C=C}$. D2 is $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, but-3-en-1-ol, it has an alkene bond. Aqueous $\text{Br}_2$ is orange. It undergoes electrophilic addition across $\text{C=C}$ to give a colourless dibromo product. So D2 decolourises bromine water from orange to colourless, D1 does not.

Final answer: Pair A: Tollens / Fehling's / acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ / acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$, A1 positive: silver mirror / brick-red ppt / orange to green / purple to colourless. OR alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$, A2 positive: yellow ppt.
Pair B: alkaline $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$, B1 positive: yellow ppt.
Pair C: 2,4-DNPH, C1 positive: red / orange / yellow ppt.
Pair D: $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$, D2 positive: orange to colourless.

hints: Think about what must stay the same and what must be different when two compounds are structural isomers.
walkthrough:
Pin down the two halves of the definition**
Same molecular formula means same numbers of each atom, for A1 and A2 both $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$. Different structural formula means the atoms are joined in a different order, here $\text{CHO}$ versus $\text{C-CO-C}$. Both parts are needed for the mark.
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.

hints: Count the longest carbon chain in B2 and locate the position of the $\text{C=O}$ group to number it correctly.
walkthrough:
Name the ketone systematically**
B2 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The longest chain has 5 carbons, so pentane. The $\text{C=O}$ is on carbon 3 if you number from either end, so pentan-3-one. The 3 is essential because pentan-2-one is a different isomer.

hints: Count carbons in the cyclobutane ring plus the methyl group, then add hydrogens to satisfy tetravalency including the $\text{OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Count atoms in D1**
The ring has 4 carbons, plus one methyl carbon attached to the same carbon as $\text{OH}$, so 5 carbons total. That carbon has no hydrogens, the other three ring carbons each have 2 hydrogens, the methyl has 3 hydrogens, plus one H in $\text{OH}$. That gives $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

hints: Look at the functional groups in D2. It has a $\text{C=C}$ bond but only one $\text{OH}$ group, so which polymerisation type using a $\text{C=C}$ bond is possible?
walkthrough:
Link monomer structure to polymer type**
D2 is $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. It has a $\text{C=C}$ double bond that can open and join to neighbours with no small molecule lost. That is addition polymerisation. Condensation needs two different functional groups in the monomer or two monomers, which is not the case here.

hints: Remember that addition polymerisation opens the $\text{C=C}$ to give a saturated $\text{C-C}$ backbone with two continuation bonds.
Think about which side chain remains unchanged on every second carbon, here the $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Build the backbone**
Take $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and open the double bond. You get $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH-}$ joined to the next unit. Draw two C atoms in the chain with a bond extending left from the first $\text{CH}_2$ and right from the $\text{CH}$, these are the continuation bonds. This backbone is the first mark.

Add the unchanged side chain**
The $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group does not react, it just hangs off the second carbon of the repeat unit. So the full unit is $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH)-}$. Check you have not added extra carbons or lost the $\text{OH}$.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH)]-}$ with two dangling bonds through the backbone carbons.

hints: Compare Fig 3.1 and Fig 3.2 above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and use Table 3.2 to see which absorption is present in E but missing in F.
walkthrough:
Spot the E only peak**
Ignore the $\text{C-H}$ peaks at $2850-3100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ which are in both. In E there are strong absorptions around $1600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and near $900-1000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. In F there is nothing significant between $1500$ and $1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Table 3.2 tells you $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C=C}$ in an alkene or aromatic compound. Since the molecule has only three carbons, alkene fits. So E contains $\text{C=C}$ which is lost on reaction.
Final answer: $\text{C=C}$ / alkene, absorption within $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ present in E's IR spectrum only.

hints: Look for the very broad, strong dip in F around $3300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ that is absent in E, and match it in Table 3.2.
walkthrough:
Spot the F only peak**
F shows a very broad, deep absorption centred near $3300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. E shows no absorption there. Table 3.2 assigns $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ $\text{O-H}$ to hydroxy, alcohol. The breadth is characteristic of hydrogen bonding in alcohols. So reaction with acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ has formed alcohol groups.
Final answer: hydroxyl / alcohol, broad absorption within $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ present in F's IR spectrum only.

hints: Recall which element gives M and M+2 peaks of almost equal height two mass units apart, and use the given m/e values to find $M_r$.
walkthrough:
Read the bromine fingerprint**
Equal height peaks at $m/e = 120$ and $122$ are the classic $^{79}\text{Br}$ and $^{81}\text{Br}$ isotope pattern, two mass units apart. The molecule contains one Br atom. The relative molecular mass is the weighted average, about $120.9$, often accepted as $121$.
Final answer: $M_r = 120.9$ / $121$

hints: Combine three clues: three carbons, $M_r$ about 121 with Br present, and a $\text{C=C}$ bond that reacts with cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$.
walkthrough:
Assemble E**
Three carbons plus one Br: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ has mass $36 + 5 + 79.9 = 120.9$, matching the mass spectrum. It must contain $\text{C=C}$ from the IR. The only sensible alkene with three carbons and Br is 3-bromoprop-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{Br}$. This also undergoes mild oxidation of the double bond to a diol, matching formation of F.

hints: Insert the formula of E you just deduced on the left and the formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{BrO}_2$ for F on the right, then check atoms balance.
walkthrough:
Complete the equation**
Cold dilute acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ supplies $[\text{O}]$ and adds two $\text{OH}$ across the double bond. So $\text{H}_2\text{O} + [\text{O}] + \text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{Br}$, which is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{BrO}_2$. Atoms balance: $\text{C}_3$, $\text{H}_7$, $\text{Br}_1$, $\text{O}_2$ on each side.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{O} + [\text{O}] + \text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{BrO}_2$

hints: Think about how to make both halves of the ester, propan-1-ol and propanoic acid, starting from the same aldehyde propanal.
Recall the specific reducing agent for aldehyde to primary alcohol and the oxidising agent for aldehyde to carboxylic acid.
Remember what catalyst is needed to react the alcohol and carboxylic acid together to form the ester C2.
walkthrough:
Make the alcohol half from A1**
Take one portion of propanal, A1. Reduce it with sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_4$, in methanol or aqueous conditions. The $\text{CHO}$ gains hydrogen to give propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{OH}$. This is the alcohol needed for the ester.

Make the acid half from A1**
Take a second portion of propanal. Oxidise it by heating with acidified potassium dichromate, $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The aldehyde is oxidised to propanoic acid, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. This is the acid needed for the ester.

Join them by esterification**
Warm the propanoic acid with propan-1-ol with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, or other concentrated mineral acid catalyst. This condensation eliminates water and forms propyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is C2.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} + [\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ propan-1-ol.
Step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} + [\text{O}] \xrightarrow{\text{acidified K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7, \text{heat}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ propanoic acid.
Step 3: acid + alcohol $\xrightarrow{\text{conc H}_2\text{SO}_4 / \text{H}^+, \text{heat}}$ propyl propanoate C2 + $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
